title: Two Pointers
tagline: Two indices walking an array turn many O(n²) scans into a single O(n) sweep.

intuition.analogy: Two people search a sorted bookshelf for a pair of books whose page counts add to a target. One starts at the thin end, the other at the thick end. If the pair is too thin, the left person steps right; too thick, the right person steps left. They converge without ever backtracking.
paragraphs: The two-pointer pattern keeps two indices that move toward each other (or in the same direction) based on a condition, so the array is processed in a single pass instead of nested loops.

On a sorted array, the opposite-ends variant exploits monotonicity: moving the left pointer can only increase a sum, moving the right can only decrease it. That gives a deterministic rule for which pointer to advance, guaranteeing every useful pair is considered.

The same-direction variant (slow/fast) is used for in-place rewriting: the slow pointer marks where the next kept element goes, the fast pointer scans ahead. It's the backbone of dedupe, partition, and compaction problems.
intuition.keyIdea: Use the structure (sorted order or a keep/skip rule) to decide which pointer to move, so each element is visited once.

steps.title: Place the pointers
steps.detail: Opposite ends (l=0, r=n-1) for pair/partition problems; both at the start (slow=fast=0) for compaction problems.

steps.title: Evaluate the condition
steps.detail: Compute the quantity of interest (e.g. a[l] + a[r]). Compare against the target to decide the move.

steps.title: Advance the correct pointer
steps.detail: If the sum is too small, l++ (need bigger); too big, r-- (need smaller); equal → record/return. They never move backward, so total moves ≤ n.

complexity.timeReason: Each pointer moves only inward and never resets, so the total number of moves is bounded by n.

pitfalls: The opposite-ends trick needs a sorted array — sort first if the problem allows it.
For duplicates, remember to skip equal neighbours to avoid repeated answers (e.g. 3Sum).
Mixing up which pointer to move flips the logic; tie it to the monotonic effect on your quantity.

dryRun.clickMoment: Each comparison eliminates an entire row/column of the implicit pair matrix. Instead of checking all ~28 pairs, five steps suffice.

problems.title: Two Sum II (sorted)
problems.statement: Return indices of two numbers in a sorted array that add to target.
problems.hint: Opposite-ends pointers; move based on the sum.

approach: Because the array is sorted, two pointers from both ends converge: if the pair sum is too small move left pointer right, if too big move right pointer left.
When the sum matches, return the 1-based indices. O(n) with no extra space.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.statement: Check if a string is a palindrome considering only alphanumerics.
problems.hint: Pointers from both ends, skip non-alphanumerics, compare.

approach: Two pointers from both ends; skip non-alphanumeric characters and compare lowercased letters.
If any mismatch occurs it is not a palindrome; pointers meeting means success. O(n).

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.statement: Find all unique triplets that sum to zero.
problems.hint: Fix one element, two-pointer the rest; skip duplicates carefully.
problems.tests: Two pointers nested inside a loop + dedup.

approach: Sort, then fix each a[i] and two-pointer the rest for pairs summing to -a[i].
Skip duplicates at the fixed index and after finding a triple to avoid repeats. O(n^2).

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.statement: Pick two lines forming a container holding the most water.
problems.hint: Move the shorter wall inward — it's the limiting factor.

approach: Water held by two lines is width × min(height). Start widest; the shorter line limits the area, so moving it inward is the only way to possibly improve.
Move the pointer at the shorter line each step, tracking the max area. O(n).

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.statement: Compute trapped rainwater given an elevation map.
problems.hint: Two pointers with running left-max and right-max; process the smaller side.

approach: Water above each bar is min(maxLeft, maxRight) - height. Two pointers track running left/right maxima from both ends.
Whichever side has the smaller running max is the binding constraint, so process that side and add its trapped water. O(n), O(1) space.
